rewrites.blindSummary:
In May 2018, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The coverage framed the act as an “abominable” one defying “the traditional laws and heritage of the land”, and no prosecution is recorded: customary moral judgement operating lethally, with complete impunity. For national context, a rights-monitoring report published in January 2025 documented 556 violations against real or perceived LGBT people affecting 850 victims across the country in 2024 — and states these are only a fraction of the true scale.

This state/province's finding is the killing itself: where a discovered visitor can face lethal “community justice” invoked in the name of tradition, answered afterwards by nobody.
rewrites.blindTangential: The documented lethal incidents here concern male same-sex conduct rather than gender expression directly; their weight for trans visitors is the demonstrated capacity for community-justice killing with impunity in a customary-authority setting.
blindSourceSummaries: A news outlet (May 2018): in a community a mob lynched one of two men caught together and the other escaped, framed as an “abominable act” under traditional heritage; documents fatal community violence in this state/province.

A rights-monitoring organisation's “2024 violations report” (published January 2025): annual documentation of violations based on real or perceived SOGIESC across the country; per the dossier, its 2024 edition records 556 violations affecting 850 victims across the reporting period and states these represent only a fraction of the true scale.

On 10 June 2010 a news outlet reported from a city in this state/province that a middle-aged man narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was caught in a same-sex act with his partner in the partner's rented apartment; a neighbour raised the alarm and he fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, which then “unleashed terror” on the partner. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution is recorded in the report, and the man's whereabouts were still unknown at filing. First incident-level evidence for this state/province beyond the 2018 killing: lethal mob “community justice” operates in the state/province capital too, with no documented law-enforcement response.

A news outlet reported on 15 August 2008 that police declared a man wanted over “gay practice” after he and his partner were caught in the act in a remote community in this state/province in February 2008; a mob mercilessly beat the two for desecrating the community, the man escaped before police arrived, and the police arrested the partner for interrogation. Direct evidence that this state/province's police machinery pursued same-sex couples on the ground in 2008 — a community lynching attempt answered by arrest and a wanted declaration rather than protection.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province sits squarely in the historic-era geography where the traditional-courts jurisdiction is most extensive following the historic-era map: a rights organisation's analysis of the traditional-leadership law identifies these areas as a “separate legal system” whose adjudication of gender and sexual matters under customary law with a consent presumption against the individual constitutes the principal sub-national legal divergence in the country. The law was declared invalid in a court ruling (2023) but suspended and extended; the replacement bill has been delayed. No state/province has religious criminal law; no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

This state/province is also the only one outside three metropolitan peers to have received its own representative hate-crime prevalence study (2010; the hosting organisation's review records only three quantitative studies ever attempted nationally), giving it a data-presence signal: incidents against queer people here are, historically, more likely to appear in research rather than only in the “dark figure” of unreported crime that characterises most state/provinces. No trans-specific incident series was found. The 2010 study covers gay and lesbian people; its relevance to a trans visitor is as a proxy for reporting culture and the volume of anti-queer violence in a traditional-authority-heavy state/province.

The score is 0.04 below the national 0.69. vs. a peer state/province (0.65), the two share the historic-era customary-authority finding at similar magnitude; this state/province's additional 2010 data presence does not raise it above the peer because the study documents violence prevalence rather than institutional response capacity. vs. another peer (0.63), this state/province sits higher because that peer adds a retrieved township queerphobia study and an alignment of a traditional monarch and a traditional-leaders' association against queer people; this state/province has the jurisdictional risk without a comparable named-authority statement. vs. two metropolitan peers (0.72 and 0.71), the gap reflects metro institutional functioning versus rural customary-authority geography. The dossier's under-reporting caveat applies equally: a state/province with more recorded hate crime may simply have better reporting than more danger.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2010 state/province-level prevalence study documents hate crime against gay and lesbian people; for a trans visitor it works as a proxy for reporting culture and the volume of anti-queer violence in a traditional-authority-heavy state/province.
blindSourceSummaries: A rights organisation (29 May 2012): the traditional-courts bill then before parliament threatened LGBT residents by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the historic-era areas; the organisation reports rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas, and the bill offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. Supports this state/province's framing of traditional-court rural jurisdiction as the defining risk factor for LGBT travellers off the main cities.

A campaign review of hate crimes (2016, hosted by one organisation and conducted with another): the companion review of hate crimes against LGBT people in the country states that only three quantitative studies have ever been done — the 2003 empowerment study across three metropolitan state/provinces; a 2010 study in this state/province; and this national campaign study — and measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

The trans community in this state/province cannot access hormone replacement therapy (HRT) at any public health facility in the state/province and residents are forced to travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to a metropolitan district of another state/province to get it, a news outlet reported on 21 February 2023. The state/province's health department confirmed it has no facilities providing HRT for transgender people, in its response to a complaint lodged by an international justice organisation with the national human-rights commission. Documents the state/province-level absence of trans-specific healthcare that a trans visitor reliant on prescribed HRT would confront on the ground.

A news outlet (23 March 2016, citing a local daily) reported that an 18-year-old lesbian from a village in this state/province was barred from attending school for refusing to wear a skirt; the principal sent her home saying she must wear a skirt “since I was a girl”, and she stayed home for three weeks without attending any classes. Records a state/province institution enforcing a gendered dress code against a gender-nonconforming pupil, illustrating the state/province's socially conservative enforcement climate.

A report on same-sex sexuality in this state/province, released in October 2010, presented the results of a survey conducted under the auspices of a university psychology centre during 2009 and 2010, with LGBT organisations collaborating; it surveyed 319 LGBT people from a largely rural background in one of the country's poorest and most under-populated state/provinces, asking about openness about same-sex sexuality, how LGBT persons perceive their environment, and sexual abuse and discrimination. Provides the state/province-level 2010 survey behind this record's data-presence signal.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province's security apparatus operates outside legal constraint on this question. In February 2017, law-enforcement and security officials launched an anti-gay purge: dozens of men were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities, starved and tortured; some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families “barely alive from beatings” after their captors exposed them to relatives encouraged to carry out honour killings (a rights organisation, 2017). Independent domestic reporting in January 2019 found the persecution resuming and the documented secret facility active again, while the regional leader's press office denied such sites exist. Since 2022, two investigations have documented detained homosexual men blackmailed into “volunteering” for front-line conscription in the war (at least seven sent, one killed) and a mass wave of unlawful detentions tied to forced mobilisation. An official country-policy note (June 2025) records systematic campaigns in this state/province and the wider region from 2017 to 2024 — abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings — and assesses trans people and visible advocates as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with such violence spreading beyond the region after the 2023 “extremist movement” designation.

For a discovered or outed visitor: detention without legal process, torture, coerced conscription or death, with no functioning judicial remedy.
rewrites.blindTangential: The documented campaigns — the 2017 purge, the conscription blackmail — targeted men perceived as homosexual; trans-specific detentions in the state/province are not separately tabulated in these sources, but the same unofficial-detention apparatus is what an official immigration assessment treats as likely to persecute trans people in the region.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Frequent terrorist attacks and general armed instability in the state/province, cited by travel advisories for all visitors, are separate from trans-specific risk.
blindSourceSummaries: A rights organisation (26 May 2017): documents the Feb 2017 local police purge — men believed gay rounded up, held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured; some forcibly disappeared, others returned to families “barely alive from beatings”, captors outing them and urging honour killings. The report shows the regional leader's denial notwithstanding that top regional officials knew. The core sourced basis for this record's extreme-risk profile.

An independent domestic news outlet (11 Jan 2019): learned of renewed persecution of gay men in this state/province — warnings circulated via social-network LGBT-group admins telling those still at large to leave the state/province; the regional leader's press secretary denied the reports. Follows the outlet's April 2017 investigation into torture and killings of gay men for which no criminal case was opened. Establishes the purge reactivated within two years, not a one-off.

A news outlet (4 Sep 2024): a regional monitoring organisation reports local security forces coercing detained gay men into military service — at least seven sent to frontlines in the war, one already killed; methods began before the 21 Sep 2022 mobilisation order. In early Sep 2022 six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned they'd be sent to the front. Establishes detention-to-frontline blackmail as an ongoing persecution vector since 2022.

A news outlet (an investigation by a human-rights centre): a mass wave of unlawful detentions sweeping this state/province with detainees forcibly sent to fight in the war — people detained over minor pretexts (missing insurance documents), taken to police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse, forced to sign contracts; families sometimes must recruit two “volunteers” to free a detained relative. Complements the gay-specific coercion reports: conscription machinery as a generalised coercive tool of the local security apparatus.

An official country-policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity (June 2025): records systematic anti-LGBT campaigns across this state/province and the wider region 2017–2024 (abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings); assesses that in the region trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; notes the 2023 “extremist organisation” designation of the international LGBT+ movement exposing support/activity to 2–6 years (organising 6–10) imprisonment, with violence spreading beyond the region. The freshest official-assessment source for the record's trans-specific claim.

rewrites.blindSummary:
An official country-policy note (June 2025) identifies the region — including this state/province — as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, documenting systematic campaigns by local and regional authorities between 2017 and 2024 including abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. A regional monitoring organisation's director states there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region”, that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, and that the situation worsens year on year.

A country's travel advisory tells travellers to avoid all travel to the parent nation, names this state/province among those where terrorist attacks are frequent, and warns that special permission from the interior ministry is required to enter certain areas — an access regime that also hampers independent monitoring of how state/province and customary authority operate on the ground.

For a visitor the risk here is the regional pattern: the national “extremist” designation of 2023, which extended violence in detention beyond the region, combined with local security structures and family-honour norms that produce extrajudicial responses unmediated by legal process. No separate state/province-specific written law targeting trans people exists, and no documented purge infrastructure on the scale reported elsewhere is attributed to this state/province.
rewrites.blindTangential: The “no safe life” assessment and the shared security-and-custom enforcement logic concern LGBTIQ+ people broadly rather than tabulating trans-specific cases in the state/province.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Advisories cite frequent terrorist attacks and instability across the region for all travellers; that general insecurity is distinct from the trans-specific exception the same advisories carve out.
blindSourceSummaries: An official country-policy note (June 2025): names the region — including this state/province — as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; documents systematic campaigns by local and regional authorities 2017–2024 (abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings); assesses trans people and visible advocates specifically. Freshest official assessment anchoring this record's regional-pattern claim.

A foreign-affairs ministry travel advisory for the parent nation (retrieved for this review): advises avoiding all travel; flags frequent terrorist attacks in several sub-national units; states special permission from the interior ministry is required to enter certain areas and regions; and warns violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons occurs, particularly in some state/provinces of the region. The record's access-regime claim (interior-ministerial permission hampering monitoring) comes from here.

A human-rights foundation interview with a regional monitoring organisation's director (working in exile): “There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families”; situation worsens year on year. Testimony-based regional assessment underpinning this record's “no safe private existence” line.

rewrites.blindSummary:
An official country-policy note (June 2025) treats the region as the exception to its general finding on the parent nation: people in the region, trans people, and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people by local and regional authorities from 2017 to 2024 included abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. A regional monitoring organisation states there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region”, where even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families.

A country's advisory against all travel to the parent nation names this state/province among those where terrorist attacks are frequent and warns that entering certain areas requires special permission from the interior ministry; the special-access regime also limits independent monitoring. Like a neighbouring state/province, this one has no documented state/province-specific purge infrastructure on the scale recorded elsewhere.

The risk for a discovered visitor is national hostility operating through local security structures and family-honour norms — extrajudicial responses unmediated by legal process — rather than any state/province-specific written provision against trans people.
rewrites.blindTangential: The named-permission regime and the “no safe life” finding apply to the state/province as part of an LGBTIQ+ group broadly; no state/province-specific trans purge infrastructure is documented.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Frequent terrorist attacks, cited for all travellers to this state/province, are a general-security factor distinct from trans risk.
blindSourceSummaries: A foreign-affairs ministry travel advisory for the parent nation (retrieved for this review): advises avoiding all travel; lists this state/province among units with frequent terrorist attacks; notes surveillance of foreigners and specifically that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, allies and families have been attacked, harassed and abused; since Jan 2024 organisations advocating for 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as “extremist”; special interior-ministry permission required to enter certain areas. Named-in-source access/security facts for this record.

A human-rights foundation interview with a regional monitoring organisation's director: “There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families”; annual deterioration attested by an on-the-ground defender working in exile. rewrites.blindSummary:
An official country-policy note (June 2025) treats the region as the exception within the parent nation: people in the region, trans people, and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, amid documented systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people from 2017 to 2024 that included abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. A regional monitoring organisation — which coordinates roughly 34 evacuations a year of people fleeing the region — states there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region”, where even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families.

No state/province-specific purge infrastructure is documented. The visitor-facing risk is therefore the regional pattern rather than any locally recorded apparatus: the 2023 national “extremist” designation, after which violence in detention spread beyond the region, operating through security practices and family-honour norms that can produce extrajudicial outcomes unmediated by legal process.
rewrites.blindTangential: The informal-enforcement pattern documented for the zone — round-ups, detention, family exposure, violence unmediated by legal process — was first recorded against gay men and LGBTIQ+ people generally rather than trans people specifically; the same security-and-custom logic operates on any discovered queer visitor, trans or not.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: The don't-travel designation for the zone is driven largely by general armed-conflict and security risk that affects all travellers; the trans-relevant content is the LGBT-specific exception drawn by an official country-policy note, not the blanket advisory level.
blindSourceSummaries: A human-rights foundation interview with a regional monitoring organisation's director: “There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families”; year-on-year deterioration from an on-the-ground defender in exile. Regional testimony underpinning this record's risk framing.
